mainTopic: קרעין שאין מתאחין: which mourning tears are never mended, the sources for each, and how to tear and stitch them
overview: This amud opens with a ברייתא that lists the tears of mourning that may never be properly sewn back together. They are for a parent, one's רבו who taught him תורה, the נשיא, the אב בית דין, bad news, ברכת השם, a burned ספר תורה, and the ruined ערי יהודה, מקדש and ירושלים. The גמרא then finds a פסוק for each case. אלישע's cry as אליהו went up to heaven teaches the rule for parents and for a רבו, and the extra words 'into two pieces' show the tear stays forever. דוד's mourning for שאול and יהונתן teaches the rule for the נשיא, the אב בית דין and bad news. Bad news here means only a disaster that strikes most of the nation. חזקיהו's officials teach the rule for ברכת השם, and יהויקים burning ירמיהו's scroll teaches the rule for a burned ספר תורה. רב הונא adds that a torn ספר תורה needs two tears, and שמואל limits this to destruction by force. Finally, the גמרא gives the פסוקים to say over the ruined cities, ירושלים and the מקדש, and settles when one tear is enough. It ends with a ברייתא allowing rough stitching but not real mending, and begins a statement of רב חסדא that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The list of tears that are never mended
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists the cases where a torn garment may never be properly sewn back together. It ends with the order of tearing for the מקדש and ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are the tears that are never mended: one who tears for his father, his mother, his teacher who taught him תורה, the נשיא, the אב בית דין, bad news, ה׳'s name being cursed, a burned ספר תורה, the ערי יהודה, the מקדש, and ירושלים. He tears for the מקדש first and then makes the tear longer for ירושלים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that lists which mourning tears may never be fully sewn back up. It also explains how to tear when one sees the ruined מקדש and ירושלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most tears of mourning may be repaired later. This list names special cases where the tear stays torn for good, because the loss is extra serious. The last line adds a practical rule: you do not make a new tear for ירושלים, you just make the מקדש tear longer.

keyTerms.meaning: Tears made in one's garment as a sign of mourning (קריעה).
The head of the Sanhedrin and leader of the Jewish people.
The head of the court, second to the נשיא.
Literally 'blessing God's name'; a polite way of saying cursing God.
Adds on, makes the existing tear longer.

steps.confusionAlert: ברכת השם here does NOT mean hearing someone bless God. It is a polite way of saying hearing someone curse God, and that is why one tears.
steps.whyThisMatters: This list is the base for the rest of the sugya. Every case on it will need a source or an explanation.

phrases.english: And these are the tears that are never mended:
One who tears for his father or for his mother,
or for his teacher who taught him Torah,

phrases.aramaic: וְעַל נָשִׂיא וְעַל אָב בֵּית דִּין,
phrases.english: or for the Nasi, or for the head of the court,
or upon hearing bad news,
or upon the 'blessing' of God's name,
phrases.notes: This is a polite way of saying someone cursed God's name.

phrases.english: or for a Torah scroll that was burned,
or upon seeing the ruined cities of Judah,
or the ruined Temple, or Jerusalem.
And he first tears for the Temple,
and then makes the tear longer for Jerusalem.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the topic with a ברייתא listing the cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In these listed cases the tear may never be properly mended. For the מקדש and ירושלים, one tears for the מקדש and lengthens the same tear for ירושלים.

steps.title: Where do we learn tearing for parents and a teacher?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that one tears for a father, a mother, and one's רבו who taught him תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: His father, his mother, and his teacher who taught him תורה: where do we learn this from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts working through the list and asks for a source for its first three cases. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא stated the rule without a source. The גמרא wants a פסוק showing that one tears for a parent and for a רבו.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know this? A request for a source.
His teacher, the one who taught him תורה.

phrases.english: His father and his mother
and his teacher who taught him Torah: from where do we learn this?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ וְרַבּוֹ שֶׁלִּימְּדוֹ תּוֹרָה מְנָלַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the first cases in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק that teaches tearing for a parent and for one's רבו.

steps.title: אלישע's cry teaches both cases
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the פסוק where אלישע cries 'My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen.' It reads 'my father' as the source for parents, and 'chariots of Israel' as the source for one's רבו.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And אלישע saw it, and he cried out: My father, my father, the chariots of ישראל and its horsemen.' 'My father, my father' refers to his father and mother. 'The chariots of ישראל and its horsemen' refers to his teacher who taught him תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with the פסוק that describes אלישע watching אליהו go up to heaven. It splits the פסוק in two: the first half is the source for parents and the second half is the source for one's רבו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'My father, my father' is said twice, so the גמרא uses it for both father and mother. The words 'chariots of Israel and its horsemen' are taken as describing a great teacher, so they teach about tearing for one's רבו.

keyTerms.meaning: The נביא who was the student of אליהו.
The chariots of Israel and its horsemen.

phrases.english: As it is written: 'And Elisha saw it, and he cried out:
phrases.notes: מלכים ב 2:12. אלישע is watching his teacher אליהו go up to heaven.

phrases.english: My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen.'
'My father, my father': this refers to his father and mother,
'The chariots of Israel and its horsemen':
this refers to his teacher who taught him Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק of אלישע: 'my father, my father' covers parents, and 'chariots of Israel and its horsemen' covers one's רבו.

steps.title: How do 'chariots' mean a teacher?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how 'the chariots of Israel and its horsemen' shows that the פסוק is talking about a teacher.
steps.simpleTranslation: How is this implied?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the last step. It is not clear how chariots and horsemen point to a רבו, and the answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'My father' clearly fits a parent, but chariots and horsemen sound military. The גמרא wants to know what in these words points to a teacher.

keyTerms.meaning: How is this implied? Where do you see this in the words?

phrases.english: How is this implied?
phrases.notes: He means: what in the words 'chariots of Israel' shows that this is a teacher?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for an explanation of the second half of the reading in step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How 'chariots of Israel and its horsemen' refers to one's רבו.

steps.title: רב יוסף's translation: a teacher's prayers protect better than an army
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings רב יוסף's Aramaic translation of the פסוק: 'My teacher, my teacher, whose prayers were better for Israel than chariots and horsemen.'
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב יוסף translates it: 'My teacher, my teacher, who was better for Israel with his prayers than chariots and horsemen.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reading using רב יוסף's Aramaic translation. That translation shows that the פסוק describes a great teacher whose prayers protected the people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף reads 'my father' as 'my teacher.' He also reads 'chariots and horsemen' as a comparison: the teacher's prayers protected Israel better than an army could. So the second half of the פסוק describes a רבו, and this supports tearing for one's teacher.

keyTerms.meaning: As he translates, referring to an Aramaic translation of a פסוק.

steps.whatToRemember: Parents and one's רבו are both learned from אלישע's cry over אליהו: 'my father' for parents, and 'chariots of Israel', explained by רב יוסף, for a teacher.

phrases.english: As Rav Yosef translates it:
'My teacher, my teacher, who was better for Israel
with his prayers than chariots and horsemen.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: According to רב יוסף's translation, the פסוק praises a teacher whose prayers protected Israel more than chariots and horsemen could.

steps.title: Where do we learn that these tears are never mended?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that these tears may never be sewn back together.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we learn that they are never mended?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא asks for the source of the main rule in the ברייתא, that these tears stay torn. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 3 showed that one tears in these cases. It did not show that the tear can never be repaired, so a second source is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: And that they are not mended.

phrases.english: And that they are never mended: from where do we learn this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the source for tearing to the source for never mending.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source that these particular tears may never be repaired.

steps.title: 'Into two pieces' means torn forever
steps.stepSummary: The same פסוק says אלישע tore his clothes 'into two pieces.' Since 'he tore them' already means into two, the extra words teach that the pieces stay apart forever.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And he took hold of his clothes and tore them into two pieces.' From the fact that it says 'and he tore them,' don't I already know it was into two? Rather, it teaches that they stay torn into two forever.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers from the continuation of the same פסוק about אלישע. The words 'into two pieces' seem extra, so it learns from them that the tear stays torn forever.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Any tear splits a cloth into two parts, so 'into two pieces' adds nothing new on a simple reading. Since the פסוק does not waste words, the גמרא reads the extra phrase as a lasting state: the garment remains two pieces and may never be sewn back properly.

keyTerms.meaning: From the fact that it says, used to show that a word is extra.
Do I not know? Meaning, this is already obvious.

steps.whatToRemember: The rule that these tears are never mended comes from the 'extra' words 'into two pieces' in the פסוק of אלישע: they stay two pieces forever.

phrases.english: As it is written: 'And he took hold of his clothes,'
phrases.notes: This is the same פסוק, מלכים ב 2:12, a few words later.

phrases.english: and tore them into two pieces.'
From the fact that it says 'and he tore them,'
don't I already know that it was into two?
Rather, it teaches that they stay torn
in two pieces forever.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב: וַיַּחֲזֵק בִּבְגָדָיו וַיִּקְרָעֵם לִשְׁנַיִם קְרָעִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra phrase 'into two pieces' teaches that the garment stays in two pieces forever, so the tear may never be mended.

steps.title: But אליהו did not die
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש challenges the proof from אלישע: אליהו is still alive, so why did אלישע tear?
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said to רבי יוחנן: Is אליהו alive?
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש pushes back on the proof from the earlier steps. אליהו went up to heaven alive, so how can אלישע's tearing teach us about mourning?
steps.deeperAnalysis: We tear clothes when someone dies. אליהו never died, so אלישע's tearing seems to have nothing to do with mourning a teacher. That would knock out the source we just learned.

keyTerms.meaning: אליהו הנביא, אלישע's teacher, who went up to heaven alive

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ לְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Reish Lakish said to Rabbi Yochanan:
Is Eliyahu alive?
phrases.notes: He means: אליהו went up in a storm and never died, so why would אלישע tear for him?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ לְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אֵלִיָּהוּ חַי הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether the פסוק about אלישע can serve as a source for tearing over a teacher's death
steps.kashyaTarget: The proof from אלישע's tearing for אליהו
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Tearing is for a death. אליהו did not die, so the case does not fit.

steps.title: To אלישע, it was as if אליהו died
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers: since אלישע never saw him again, for אלישע it counts as a death.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Since it is written 'and he saw him no more,' as far as אלישע was concerned, it was like אליהו was dead.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן defends the proof. For אלישע, losing אליהו forever was the same as losing him to death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק itself says אלישע 'saw him no more.' From אלישע's side, his teacher was gone for good, just like a death. So the case still works as a source for tearing over a רבו.

keyTerms.meaning: And he saw him no more
As far as he (אלישע) was concerned
He is like someone who died

phrases.english: He said to him,
since it is written: "And he saw him no more,"
phrases.notes: מלכים ב 2:12

phrases.english: with regard to him, he is like one who is dead.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers ריש לקיש's challenge
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the situation from the mourner's point of view
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since אליהו did not die, tearing for him does not fit the rule about tearing for a death
steps.terutzMaskana: Since אלישע would never see אליהו again, it counted as a death for him, so the proof stands
steps.whatToRemember: The source for tearing over one's רבו stands. For אלישע, losing אליהו forever was like losing him to death.

steps.title: Where do we learn to tear for a נשיא, an אב בית דין, and bad news?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves to a new set of cases and asks for their source.
steps.simpleTranslation: A נשיא, an אב בית דין, and bad news: from where do we know these?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It asks how we know that one tears clothes when a נשיא or an אב בית דין dies, or when one hears terrible news.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now we learned about parents and one's רבו. Now the גמרא asks for a source for three new cases: two leaders and a national disaster.

keyTerms.meaning: The head of the Jewish people / the סנהדרין
The head of the court, second to the נשיא
Terrible news (about a disaster to the Jewish people)

phrases.english: A Nasi and the head of the court
and bad news, from where do we derive them?
phrases.notes: The word 'tearing' is assumed: from where do we know we must tear for these?

steps.triggerLanguage: נָשִׂיא וְאַב בֵּית דִּין וּשְׁמוּעוֹת הָרָעוֹת מְנָלַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new list of cases that require tearing
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source for tearing over a נשיא, an אב בית דין, and bad news

steps.title: דוד tears for שאול and יהונתן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the פסוק where דוד and his men tore their clothes and mourned for שאול, יהונתן, and the Jewish people.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And דוד took hold of his clothes and tore them, and so did all the men with him. And they mourned, cried, and fasted until evening for שאול, for his son יהונתן, for the people of ה׳, and for the house of ישראל, because they fell by the sword.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק. דוד tore his clothes when he heard about the deaths of שאול and יהונתן and Israel's defeat in battle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק lists several groups that דוד mourned for. Each one will match one of the three cases in the question. The next step explains the matching.

keyTerms.meaning: שאול המלך, the first king of Israel

phrases.english: As it is written: "And David took hold of his clothes,
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 1:11–12

phrases.aramaic: וַיִּקְרָעֵם וְגַם כׇּל הָאֲנָשִׁים אֲשֶׁר אִתּוֹ.
phrases.english: and tore them, and also all the men who were with him.
And they mourned, and wept, and fasted until evening
for Saul and for Jonathan his son

phrases.aramaic: וְעַל עַם ה׳ וְעַל בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל
phrases.english: and for the people of God and for the house of Israel
because they fell by the sword."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the שאלה with a פסוק
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: דוד's tearing over שאול, יהונתן, and the people of ה׳ is the source

steps.title: Matching each part of the פסוק to a case
steps.stepSummary: שאול stands for the נשיא, יהונתן for the אב בית דין, and the people of ה׳ for bad news.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'שאול' is the נשיא. 'יהונתן' is the אב בית דין. 'For the people of ה׳ and the house of ישראל' is bad news.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the פסוק covers all three cases by linking each name in it to one case from the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שאול was the top leader, like a נשיא. יהונתן was second to him, like an אב בית דין. The mourning for the people who fell is mourning over a national disaster, which is 'bad news.'

phrases.english: "Saul": this is the Nasi,
"Jonathan": this is the head of the court,
"for the people of God and for the house of Israel":
these are bad news.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the פסוק from the previous step answers each part of the question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שאול = נשיא, יהונתן = אב בית דין, people of ה׳ = bad news

steps.title: Maybe you tear only when all of these happen together
steps.stepSummary: רב בר שבא suggests that maybe tearing is required only when all these tragedies happen at once, like in דוד's case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב בר שבא said to רב כהנא: But say that one tears only when all of them happen together!
steps.whatsHappening: רב בר שבא challenges the proof. In דוד's story everything happened at once, so maybe we tear only for a huge combined disaster like that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק describes one event with many losses together. That does not obviously prove that each loss alone is enough. Maybe only the whole combination calls for tearing.

keyTerms.meaning: Only when all of them happen together

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב בַּר שַׁבָּא לְרַב כָּהֲנָא:
phrases.english: Rav bar Shaba said to Rav Kahana:
But say: not until all of them happen!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב בַּר שַׁבָּא לְרַב כָּהֲנָא: וְאֵימָא עַד דְּהָווּ כּוּלְּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether the פסוק proves each case separately
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that each case alone requires tearing
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק describes all the losses together, so maybe only the combination requires tearing

steps.title: The repeated word 'for' separates each case
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא answers: the פסוק repeats 'for' before each one, which splits them into separate reasons.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The repeated 'for... for...' splits up the matter.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא answers the challenge. The פסוק says 'for' before each item, which shows that each is its own reason to tear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have said 'for שאול, יהונתן, and the people' in one list. Instead it repeats 'for' each time. That breaks the list apart, so each tragedy alone requires tearing.

phrases.english: He said to him:
"For," "for" separated the matter.
phrases.notes: The פסוק says 'for שאול, and for יהונתן, and for the people.' Each new 'for' starts a separate reason.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב בר שבא's challenge
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading from the wording of the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Tearing might be required only when all the tragedies happen together
steps.terutzMaskana: The repeated 'for' splits the list, so each tragedy alone requires tearing
steps.whatToRemember: One tears for a נשיא, for an אב בית דין, and for terrible news, and each one alone is enough. We learn this from דוד's mourning, where the repeated word 'for' separates the cases.

steps.title: Did שמואל not tear for terrible news?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rule from Step 12 that we tear for bad news. שמואל did not tear when he heard that שבור מלכא killed twelve thousand Jews.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do we really tear for bad news? People told שמואל that King שבור killed twelve thousand Jews in מזיגת קיסרי, and he did not tear!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the rule that we tear for bad news. It points to a story where שמואל heard very bad news and did not tear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 learned from the פסוק that bad news requires tearing. If that were true, שמואל should have torn when he heard about a huge massacre. His silence suggests that bad news alone does not require tearing.

phrases.english: But do we really tear for bad news?
But didn't they say to Shmuel:
King Shapur killed
twelve thousand Jews in Mezigat Caesarea,
phrases.notes: מזיגת קיסרי is the name of a place.

phrases.english: and he did not tear!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the bad-news rule learned in Step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that one tears clothes on hearing bad news
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל heard about a massacre of twelve thousand Jews and did not tear. So bad news alone must not require tearing.

steps.title: Only when most of the community is struck
steps.stepSummary: Tearing for bad news is required only when the disaster hits most of the Jewish people, like the disaster in שאול's time.
steps.simpleTranslation: The rule was said only when the disaster struck most of the community, like the event that happened with שאול.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the rule. You tear only for a disaster that hits most of the Jewish people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The massacre told to שמואל was terrible, but it did not strike most of the nation. The model for this rule is the defeat in דוד's פסוק, where the whole nation of Israel was struck. So שמואל's not tearing fits the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: They only said it when… (limits a rule)

steps.whatToRemember: Tearing for bad news applies only to a national disaster that strikes most of the Jewish people, like the defeat in שאול's time.

phrases.english: They said it only when it is the majority of the community
and like the event that happened.
phrases.notes: This means the story of שאול's death and the nation's defeat, from the פסוק in Step 11.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא אָמְרוּ אֶלָּא בְּרוֹב צִבּוּר וּכְמַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁהָיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any bad news, even a massacre in one place, requires tearing.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a disaster that strikes most of the nation, like the one in שאול's time, requires tearing.

steps.title: Did שבור ever kill Jews?
steps.stepSummary: A side question: the story says שבור killed Jews, yet שבור himself told שמואל he never killed a Jew.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did King שבור really kill Jews? But King שבור told שמואל: 'May a blessing come to me, for I never killed a Jew!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes off on a side point. It questions the story itself, because שבור claimed he never killed any Jew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 said שבור killed twelve thousand Jews. That seems to contradict שבור's own claim that he never killed a Jew. The גמרא needs to fit the two reports together.

phrases.english: But did King Shapur really kill Jews?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא אֲמַר לֵיהּ שַׁבּוּר מַלְכָּא לִשְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: But didn't King Shapur say to Shmuel:
May it come to me
phrases.notes: He means: I deserve a blessing for this.

phrases.english: that I have never killed a Jew!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי קְטַל שַׁבּוּר מַלְכָּא יְהוּדָאֵי? וְהָא אֲמַר לֵיהּ שַׁבּוּר מַלְכָּא לִשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side challenge to the story quoted in Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The report that שבור killed twelve thousand Jews
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שבור said he never killed a Jew, so how could he have killed twelve thousand?

steps.title: They brought it on themselves
steps.stepSummary: In that case the Jews caused their own deaths. As רבי אמי says, their rebellion led to the walls of לודקיא being broken.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, they caused it themselves. As רבי אמי said: because of the sound of the harp strings of מזיגת קיסרי, the wall of לודקיא burst.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that שבור did not start the killing. The people brought it on themselves by rebelling against him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שבור's claim means he never chose to kill Jews on his own. In מזיגת קיסרי the people rebelled, so the killing was a reaction to their actions. רבי אמי describes this in an exaggerated picture: the noise of their celebrating broke the city walls.

phrases.english: There, they brought it upon themselves,
as Rabbi Ami said:
Because of the sound of the harp strings of Mezigat Caesarea,
the wall of Laodicea burst.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the side challenge of Step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the two reports by cause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שבור killed Jews on his own initiative, which contradicts his claim.
steps.terutzMaskana: שבור never started killing Jews. In מזיגת קיסרי the Jews' rebellion brought the killing on themselves.

steps.title: Source for tearing on hearing ה׳'s name cursed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the ברייתא and asks for the source that one tears on hearing ברכת השם, a polite way of saying cursing ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: For hearing ה׳'s name 'blessed' (meaning cursed), from where do we learn that one tears?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the list of cases in the ברייתא from step 1 and asks for the source of the next one. This step sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The next item on the list is hearing ה׳'s name cursed. The text calls it 'blessing' so as not to say the ugly word outright. The גמרא wants a פסוק that shows tearing in this case.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Blessing' ה׳'s name, a polite way of saying cursing ה׳
From where do we learn this?

steps.confusionAlert: Here ברכת השם does not mean blessing ה׳. It is a polite way of saying the opposite: cursing ה׳.

phrases.english: For the 'blessing' of the Name, from where do we know?
phrases.notes: 'Blessing' is a polite way to say cursing ה׳.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the side discussion about שבור to the list of cases in the ברייתא of step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A scriptural source for tearing on hearing ה׳'s name cursed

steps.title: חזקיהו's officials came with torn clothes
steps.stepSummary: The source is the פסוק in which אליקים, שבנא, and יואח came to חזקיהו with torn clothes after hearing רבשקה's insults against ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And אליקים son of חלקיה, who was over the household, and שבנא the scribe, and יואח son of אסף the recorder came to חזקיהו with their clothes torn.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק showing officials who tore their clothes after hearing ה׳ insulted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These officials had just heard רבשקה speak against ה׳. They came to the king with torn clothes. Their tearing serves as the model for tearing whenever one hears ה׳'s name cursed.

phrases.english: As it is written: "And Eliakim son of Hilkiya came,
phrases.notes: מלכים ב 18:37

phrases.english: who was over the household,
and Shebna the scribe,
and Joah son of Asaph the recorder,
to Hezekiah with their clothes torn."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the source question of Step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The officials of חזקיהו tore their clothes on hearing ה׳ insulted, which teaches that one tears on hearing ברכת השם.

steps.title: Who must tear on hearing ה׳ cursed
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches two things. Both the one who hears the curse and the one who hears it secondhand must tear. Witnesses who repeat it in court need not tear again, since they already tore when they first heard it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: both the one who hears it and the one who hears it from the one who heard it must tear. The witnesses do not need to tear, because they already tore when they first heard it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that spells out who must tear when ה׳'s name is cursed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The duty is not only for the person who heard the curse directly. Even someone who hears it repeated must tear. Witnesses who repeat the curse in court are exempt then, because they already tore when they first heard it.

keyTerms.meaning: One who hears from the mouth of the one who heard

steps.whatToRemember: Hearing ה׳ cursed, even secondhand, requires tearing. Witnesses do not tear again in court because they already tore the first time.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Both one who hears
and one who hears from the mouth of the one who heard
is obligated to tear.
But the witnesses are not obligated to tear,
phrases.notes: This means when they repeat the curse in court as testimony.

phrases.english: because they already tore at the time they heard it.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֶחָד הַשּׁוֹמֵעַ וְאֶחָד הַשּׁוֹמֵעַ מִפִּי הַשּׁוֹמֵעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds details about who must tear for ברכת השם, the case sourced in Step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both a direct and a secondhand hearer of a curse against ה׳ must tear. Witnesses are exempt when they testify, since they already tore.

steps.title: Why not tear again when hearing it in court?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rule that witnesses need not tear again. They are hearing the curse again right now.
steps.simpleTranslation: What difference does it make that they tore when they first heard it? They are hearing it again now!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the ברייתא's rule that witnesses repeating the curse in court don't tear again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each hearing of a curse against ה׳ should seem to require a new tear. Having torn once before does not obviously cancel the new hearing happening now.

phrases.english: What difference does it make that they tore at the time they heard it?
But they are hearing it now!

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁשָּׁמְעוּ מַאי הָוֵי? הָא קָא שָׁמְעִי הַשְׁתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the second rule of the ברייתא in step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that witnesses in court do not tear again.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A new hearing should require a new tear, regardless of an earlier tear.

steps.title: Only the king tore, not the messengers
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says only חזקיהו tore when he heard. The messengers who repeated it to him did not tear again.
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't think that. It says: 'When King חזקיהו heard, he tore his clothes.' The king tore, but they did not tear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers from the פסוק: when the messengers repeated the curse to חזקיהו, only he tore, not them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The messengers had already torn when they first heard רבשקה. The פסוק mentions only the king tearing, so someone who already tore does not tear again when he repeats the words.

keyTerms.meaning: don't think that; it can't enter your mind

steps.whatToRemember: One who already tore over ברכת השם does not tear again when repeating it, as with the messengers to חזקיהו.

phrases.english: Don't even think that,
as it is written:
"And it was, when King Hezekiah heard,
phrases.notes: מלכים ב 19:1

phrases.english: he tore his clothes"
the king tore, but they did not tear.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 22.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every new hearing requires a new tear.
steps.terutzMaskana: Someone who already tore does not tear again when he repeats the curse.

steps.title: Source that these tears are never sewn up
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of the ברייתא's rule that tears for ברכת השם may not be properly sewn back.
steps.simpleTranslation: And that these tears are not sewn back together, from where do we know it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a source for another detail of the ברייתא. It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing about חזקיהו's tearing says the tear must stay open forever. So a separate source is needed.

phrases.english: And that they are not sewn back, from where do we know?
phrases.notes: The ברייתא said tears for hearing ה׳ cursed may never be sewn back properly.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to another detail of the same ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that these tears are permanent.

steps.title: Learned from the word 'tearing'
steps.stepSummary: The rule comes from a גזירה שוה. The word 'tearing' here is linked to the same word elsewhere, where the tear is permanent.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is learned from 'tearing' and 'tearing.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a גזירה שוה, matching the word for tearing in two places.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the other place where the word appears, the tear is permanent. The shared word carries that rule over to tearing for ברכת השם.

keyTerms.meaning: learning a law from the same word used in two places

phrases.english: It is learned from "tearing" and "tearing."
phrases.notes: The other 'tearing' is when אלישע tore his clothes for אליהו, a tear that was never sewn back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה from the word 'tearing.'

steps.title: Source for tearing over a burned ספר תורה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that one tears his clothes when a ספר תורה is burned.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ספר תורה that was burned, from where do we know that one tears?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next case in the ברייתא, tearing over a burned ספר תורה, and asks for its source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new topic within the list of reasons to tear. Like the last case, it needs a פסוק to back it up.

phrases.english: A Torah scroll that was burned, from where do we know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to a new case of tearing.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source requiring tearing over a burned ספר תורה.

steps.title: יהויקים burned ירמיהו's scroll
steps.stepSummary: The source is the פסוק describing how the scroll was cut and thrown into the fire as יהודי read it to the king.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'When יהודי read three or four columns, he cut it with a scribe's knife and threw it into the fire in the firepan, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the פסוק about the burning of ירמיהו's scroll as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This פסוק describes the scroll being cut and burned. The actual proof comes from the next פסוק (ירמיהו 36:24), which the גמרא quotes in step 31. There the people are blamed for not tearing their clothes, which shows they should have torn.

phrases.english: As it is written:
"And it was, when Jehudi read
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 36:23

phrases.english: three or four columns,
he would cut it with the scribe's knife
and throw it into the fire
that was in the firepan, etc."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 26.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק about the burning of ירמיהו's scroll.

steps.title: What are 'three or four columns'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the פסוק means by 'three or four columns.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What is meant by 'three or four columns'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses on a phrase in the פסוק it just quoted and asks what it means. The answer, a story, comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a side question about the פסוק itself, not about the law of tearing. It asks why the scroll was cut at that point.

phrases.english: What is "three or four columns"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a phrase in the פסוק from step 27.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of 'three or four columns.'

steps.title: יהויקים hears the first verses of איכה
steps.stepSummary: יהויקים is told ירמיהו wrote a book of lamentations. After each of the first four פסוקים read to him, he answers, 'I am king.'
steps.simpleTranslation: They told יהויקים: ירמיהו wrote a book of lamentations. He asked: What is written in it? 'How does she sit alone.' He said: I am king. 'She weeps bitterly at night.' I am king. 'Judah went into exile from suffering.' I am king. 'The roads of Zion mourn.' I am king.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story to explain the 'three or four columns.' Four פסוקים of איכה are read to יהויקים, and he brushes off each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'columns' are read here as the opening פסוקים of איכה. Each time, יהויקים insists that as king these warnings don't apply to him. The story is building toward the moment he cuts the scroll.

keyTerms.meaning: king of יהודה in ירמיהו's time

phrases.english: They said to Jehoiakim:
Jeremiah wrote a book of lamentations.
He said to them: What is written in it?
"How does she sit alone."
phrases.notes: איכה 1:1

phrases.english: He said to them: I am king.
phrases.notes: He means: I'm still on the throne, so this doesn't apply to me.

phrases.english: He said to him: "She weeps bitterly at night."
I am king.
"Judah went into exile from suffering."
I am king.
"The roads of Zion mourn."
I am king.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ לִיהוֹיָקִים: כָּתַב יִרְמְיָה סֵפֶר קִינוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering step 28 through a story.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The 'columns' are the first four פסוקים of איכה read to יהויקים, each dismissed with 'I am king.'

steps.title: The fifth פסוק and the burning of ה׳'s names
steps.stepSummary: After hearing the fifth פסוק and learning that ה׳ said it, יהויקים cut out all the names of ה׳ from the scroll and burned them.
steps.simpleTranslation: They read him: 'Her enemies have become the head.' He asked: Who said this? They answered: 'For ה׳ afflicted her for her many sins.' Right away he cut out every name of ה׳ in the scroll and burned them in the fire.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing the story it began in step 29, which explains the 'three or four columns.' This is the moment the scroll was cut and burned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first four פסוקים did not bother יהויקים, because he was still king. The fifth פסוק hinted that his enemies would take over, and when he heard that ה׳ was the one saying it, he reacted by cutting out and burning ה׳'s names.

keyTerms.meaning: Afflicted her, brought suffering on her

phrases.english: "Her enemies have become the head."
phrases.notes: איכה 1:5. This is the fifth פסוק, right after the four he brushed off in step 29.

phrases.english: He said to them: Who said this?
"For ה׳ afflicted her for her many sins."
Immediately he cut out all the names of ה׳ in it,
and burned them in the fire.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues and completes the answer from step 29 about the 'three or four columns.'
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The fifth פסוק led יהויקים to cut out and burn the names of ה׳.

steps.title: They did not tear, so they should have torn
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק criticizes the king's servants for not tearing their clothes. This shows that tearing is required when a holy scroll is burned.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what the פסוק means: 'And they were not afraid, and they did not tear their clothes.' This shows that they really should have torn them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the story back to its main question from step 26: what is the source for tearing over a burned ספר תורה? The פסוק blames them for not tearing, so tearing was required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק does not command tearing directly. Instead, the proof comes from criticism: if they are blamed for not tearing, then tearing must have been the right thing to do.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what is written

steps.whatToRemember: The source for tearing over a burned ספר תורה is that the פסוק in ירמיהו criticizes the people who did not tear.

phrases.english: And this is what is written:
"And they were not afraid, and did not tear
their clothes"
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 36:24

phrases.english: which shows that they were required to tear.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the story from steps 29-30 to prove the rule asked about in step 26.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that one tears his clothes when a ספר תורה is burned.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ירמיהו 36:24, which criticizes them for not tearing their clothes.

steps.title: Maybe the tearing was for the bad news
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא suggests that they should have torn because of the terrible news in the scroll, and not because the scroll was burned.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to אביי: Maybe they had to tear because of the bad news, not because of the burning.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא challenges the proof from step 31. He offers a different reason why they should have torn.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hearing terrible news is also a reason to tear. If that was the reason here, the פסוק would prove nothing about tearing over a burned ספר תורה.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to Abaye:
Say it was because of the bad news.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the proof drawn in step 31.
steps.kashyaTarget: The proof that the tearing in ירמיהו 36:24 was for the burned scroll.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: There is another possible reason to tear, the bad news in the scroll, so the פסוק does not prove the rule.

steps.title: The bad news had not happened yet
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the bad news was only a prophecy about the future. At that time nothing bad had happened, so the tearing must have been for the burning.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Was there any bad news at that time?!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי defends the proof by rejecting רב פפא's other reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The scroll was predicting a future disaster that had not happened yet. Since there was no actual bad news to tear over, the only reason left is the burning of the holy scroll, so the proof stands.

phrases.english: He said to him:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁמוּעוֹת רָעוֹת בְּהָהִיא שַׁעְתָּא מִי הֲווֹ?!
phrases.english: Was there any bad news at that time?!

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמוּעוֹת רָעוֹת בְּהָהִיא שַׁעְתָּא מִי הֲווֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 32.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejects the other possible reason based on timing
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The tearing could have been for the terrible news in the scroll.
steps.terutzMaskana: There was no real bad news yet, so the tearing must have been for the burned scroll.

steps.title: Two tears for a torn ספר תורה
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that one who sees a torn ספר תורה makes two tears, one for the parchment and one for the writing, based on a פסוק that lists both.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חלבו said in the name of רב הונא: Someone who sees a ספר תורה that was torn must make two tears, one for the parchment and one for the writing. As it says: 'after the king burned the scroll and the words.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a new rule about tearing over a damaged ספר תורה. You do not tear just once. You tear twice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק names two separate things that were burned, 'the scroll' and 'the words.' So each one gets its own tear: the parchment is holy, and the writing on it is holy too.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a practical rule: damage to a ספר תורה calls for two separate tears.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חֶלְבּוֹ אָמַר רַב הוּנָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chelbo said in the name of Rav Huna:
One who sees a Torah scroll that was torn
is obligated to make two tears:

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד עַל הַגְּוִיל וְאֶחָד עַל הַכְּתָב,
phrases.english: one for the parchment and one for the writing,
as it says:
"after the king burned
the scroll and the words."
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 36:27. Two things are named here, the scroll and the words, and that is why there are two tears.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֶלְבּוֹ אָמַר רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further detail about tearing over a ספר תורה, using the same story of יהויקים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who sees a torn ספר תורה makes two tears, one for the parchment and one for the writing.

steps.title: רבי אבא's תפילין and the ostrich
steps.stepSummary: A story begins: רבי אבא took off his head תפילין and put them on a cushion so he could go to the bathroom, and an ostrich came and tried to swallow them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא and רב הונא בר חייא were sitting before רבי אבא. He needed to go to the bathroom, so he took off his head תפילין and put them on the cushion. An ostrich came and tried to swallow them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story. This step only sets up the situation, and what happens next continues in the following lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far we only have the setup: holy תפילין are in danger of being destroyed by an animal. The story seems to connect to the theme of damage to holy objects, and the outcome comes next.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אַבָּא וְרַב הוּנָא בַּר חִיָּיא
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiyya
were sitting before Rabbi Abba.
He needed to relieve himself,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the teacher they were sitting before.

phrases.english: he took off his head tefillin
and put it on the cushion.
An ostrich came
and wanted to swallow it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אַבָּא וְרַב הוּנָא בַּר חִיָּיא הָווּ יָתְבִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a story about holy objects in danger of destruction. Steps 36-38 complete it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setup only: the תפילין are in danger of being swallowed by an ostrich.

steps.title: רבי אבא thinks he would have needed two tears
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא says that if the ostrich had swallowed his תפילין, he would have been required to make two tears.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Now, if it had swallowed them, I would have had to make two tears.
steps.whatsHappening: The ostrich story from the last step ends with רבי אבא's comment. He thinks losing the תפילין this way would have required two tears.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבא applies רב הונא's rule from step 34: one tear for the parchment and one for the writing. He assumes this rule covers any destruction of a holy object, even by an animal.

phrases.english: He said: Now,
phrases.notes: He means: if the ostrich had actually swallowed the תפילין.

phrases.english: I would have been obligated in two tears.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר: הַשְׁתָּא כִּי חַיְּיבַן לִי שְׁתֵּי קְרִיעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the ostrich story by applying רב הונא's two-tear rule to it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אבא assumes that losing תפילין to an animal would require two tears, one for the parchment and one for the writing.

steps.title: Where do you get that from?
steps.stepSummary: Someone challenges רבי אבא and asks for his source.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: From where do you get this?
steps.whatsHappening: Someone challenges רבי אבא's assumption. This question sets up the next step, where he explains why he disagrees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is not a request for information. It signals that the speaker thinks רבי אבא has stretched the tearing rule too far.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do you get this?

phrases.english: He said to him: From where do you have this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אבא's claim from the previous step.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבא's assumption that he would need two tears if an animal destroyed his תפילין.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It asks for a source, which hints that the tearing rule does not cover this kind of case.

steps.title: שמואל: tearing applies only to destruction by force
steps.stepSummary: The challenger tells of his own similar case. רב יהודה told him in the name of שמואל that one tears only when a holy object is destroyed by force, like the king burning the scroll.
steps.simpleTranslation: I had this exact case. I went to רב מתנה, and he did not know the answer. I went to רב יהודה, and he told me that שמואל said: The rule applies only when the object is destroyed by force, like the story that happened.
steps.whatsHappening: The challenger rejects רבי אבא's claim. He brings a ruling from שמואל that limits when one must tear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tearing for a destroyed holy object applies only when it is destroyed by force (בזרוע), like יהויקים burning the scroll in step 30. An ostrich swallowing תפילין is not that kind of act, so no tearing would have been required.

keyTerms.meaning: He did not have the answer
Like the incident that happened (the king burning the scroll)

steps.whatToRemember: According to שמואל, one tears over a destroyed holy object only when it is destroyed by force, like יהויקים's burning of the scroll, and not through an accident such as an animal.
steps.whyThisMatters: This limits רב הונא's two-tear rule to cases of deliberate, violent destruction.

phrases.english: But there was an incident with me myself,
and I came before Rav Mattana,
and he did not have it in hand.
phrases.notes: He means רב מתנה did not have an answer ready.

phrases.english: I came before Rav Yehuda,
and he said to me: This is what Shmuel said:
They said it only when it is by force,
and like the incident that happened.
phrases.notes: This points back to the king cutting and burning the scroll in step 30.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge by bringing שמואל's ruling, which rejects רבי אבא's claim.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רבי אבא's view that an animal destroying תפילין would require tearing.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבי אבא did not limit the tearing rule to violent destruction like the case of יהויקים.

steps.title: What is the source for tearing over the cities of Judah?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that one tears upon seeing the cities of Judah in ruins.
steps.simpleTranslation: The cities of Judah: from where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new item on the list of things one tears for: the destroyed cities of Judah. This question sets up the פסוק in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the topic was tearing over holy scrolls. Now the גמרא looks for a source for tearing over a place, the ruined ערי יהודה.

phrases.english: The cities of Judah, from where do we know?
phrases.notes: He means: how do we know one tears upon seeing them in ruins?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: tearing over destroyed places.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source in the פסוקים for tearing upon seeing the destroyed cities of Judah.

steps.title: Men came with torn clothes
steps.stepSummary: The source is a פסוק in ירמיהו describing eighty men who came with shaved beards and torn clothes.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'Men came from Shechem, from Shiloh, and from Samaria, eighty men with shaved beards and torn clothes, cutting themselves, with offerings and frankincense in their hands, to bring to the house of ה׳.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק that shows people tearing their clothes over the destruction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These men passed through the ruined cities of Judah on their way. Their torn clothes show that people tore when they saw that destruction.

keyTerms.meaning: With shaved beards (a sign of mourning)

phrases.english: As it is written: "And men came from Shechem,
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 41:5

phrases.english: from Shiloh and from Samaria, eighty men,
with shaved beards and torn clothes,
and cutting themselves, with offerings and frankincense in their hand,
to bring to the house of ה׳, etc."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from the previous step.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק in ירמיהו 41:5 describes men with torn clothes coming past the destroyed cities, which shows that one tears over them.

steps.title: What to say and tear for the cities, Jerusalem, and the Temple
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר teaches that a person who sees the cities of Judah, ירושלים, or the בית המקדש in ruins says a fitting פסוק and tears.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חלבו said that עולא בירָאָה said that רבי אלעזר said: One who sees the cities of Judah in ruins says, 'Your holy cities have become a wilderness,' and tears. One who sees ירושלים in ruins says, 'Zion has become a wilderness, ירושלים a desolation,' and tears. One who sees the בית המקדש in ruins says, 'Our holy and glorious house, where our fathers praised You, has been burned by fire, and all our precious things have become ruins,' and tears.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר gives three levels of destruction. For each one, a person says a matching פסוק and then tears.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each place gets its own פסוק, which a person says before tearing. The order rises in holiness: first the cities of Judah, then ירושלים, then the בית המקדש.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the practice of tearing, with these פסוקים, when seeing the ruins of ירושלים and the place of the מקדש.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חֶלְבּוֹ אָמַר עוּלָּא בִּירָאָה
phrases.english: Rabbi Chelbo said that Ulla Bira'a said
that Rabbi Elazar said:
One who sees the cities of Judah in their destruction says:
"Your holy cities have become a wilderness," and he tears.
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 64:9

phrases.english: Jerusalem in its destruction, he says:
phrases.notes: The words 'one who sees' are understood here from the line before.

phrases.english: "Zion has become a wilderness,
Jerusalem a desolation," and he tears.
The Holy Temple in its destruction, he says:
"Our holy and glorious house,
where our fathers praised You,
has been burned by fire,
and all our precious things have become ruins," and he tears.
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 64:10

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֶלְבּוֹ אָמַר עוּלָּא בִּירָאָה אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the source for tearing by adding what one says and adding ירושלים and the מקדש.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For each of the cities of Judah, ירושלים, and the בית המקדש, one says the matching פסוק and then tears.

steps.title: Tear for the Temple and extend it for Jerusalem
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes again the ruling of the opening ברייתא: one tears for the מקדש and then lengthens the same tear for ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: He tears for the מקדש and adds on for ירושלים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes again the last line of the ברייתא from step 1: one tear for the מקדש, lengthened for ירושלים. This sets up the contradiction in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to this ברייתא, one tear is enough for both places. The tear for ירושלים is just an extension of the tear for the מקדש.

phrases.english: He tears for the Temple,
and adds on for Jerusalem.
phrases.notes: He makes the same tear longer instead of making a new one.

steps.triggerLanguage: קוֹרֵעַ עַל מִקְדָּשׁ, וּמוֹסִיף עַל יְרוּשָׁלַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the closing line of the ברייתא in step 1 in order to challenge it with another ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A single tear is made for the מקדש and extended for ירושלים.

steps.title: Another teaching says two separate tears
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא contrasts this with another ברייתא saying that at צופים one tears separately for the מקדש and for ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: They contrasted it with another teaching: Whether he hears or sees, once he reaches צופים he tears. He tears for the מקדש by itself and for ירושלים by itself!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא that seems to contradict the one before it. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא says to make one tear and extend it. This ברייתא says to make two separate tears, so the two teachings seem to clash.

keyTerms.meaning: And they contrasted them (a contradiction from another source)
Tzofim, a lookout point near ירושלים

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two teachings. The first says one tear for the מקדש that is then extended for ירושלים. The second says two separate tears.

phrases.english: And they contrasted them:
Both one who hears and one who sees,
once he reaches Tzofim, he tears,
and he tears for the Temple by itself
and for Jerusalem by itself!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the previous ברייתא with a conflicting one.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that one tear for the מקדש is extended for ירושלים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another ברייתא requires separate tears for the מקדש and for ירושלים, which contradicts making a single extended tear.

steps.title: It depends on which place you reach first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves the contradiction between the two ברייתות. If a person reaches the מקדש first, he lengthens that tear for ירושלים. If he reaches ירושלים first, he must make a separate tear for the מקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not difficult. This ברייתא is talking about someone who came upon the מקדש first. That ברייתא is talking about someone who came upon ירושלים first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction from the last step. It says each ברייתא is talking about a different order of arriving.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא that says 'lengthen the same tear' is talking about someone who saw the מקדש first. He already tore for the greater loss, so he only adds to that tear for ירושלים. The ברייתא that says 'tear separately' is talking about someone who saw ירושלים first. The tear he made for the lesser loss cannot cover the greater loss of the מקדש, so he needs a new tear.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; this opens an answer that removes a contradiction
This one ... that one; it splits two sources into two different cases

steps.whatToRemember: The order matters. מקדש first: one tear, and you lengthen it for ירושלים. ירושלים first: two separate tears.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the two ברייתות really argue. Each one is right, just for a different order of arriving.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
This is where he came upon the Temple first.
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא that says to lengthen the same tear for ירושלים.

phrases.english: That is where he came upon Jerusalem first.
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא about צופים that says to tear separately for each.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא דְּפָגַע בַּמִּקְדָּשׁ בְּרֵישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 43
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each ברייתא is set in a different order of arriving
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות seemed to disagree about whether the מקדש and ירושלים need one tear or two.
steps.terutzMaskana: Seeing the מקדש first means one tear that gets lengthened. Seeing ירושלים first means a separate tear for the מקדש.

steps.title: Loose stitching is allowed but proper mending is not
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that for all these special tears, a person may tack, hem, gather, or loosely stitch the torn edges together. He may not mend them properly.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: For all of these tears, one may tack them, hem them, gather them, and stitch them in a ladder-like way, but one may not mend them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about what a person may do with these torn garments afterward. It lists rough kinds of stitching that are allowed and forbids a real repair.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are tears that must never be fully repaired. The ברייתא still lets a person hold the cloth together with rough, uneven stitches so the garment can be used. The one thing forbidden is a proper, neat mending that would make the tear disappear.

keyTerms.meaning: To tack them together with loose, wide stitches
To hem them, folding and stitching the edges
To gather them, pulling the edges together
To mend them properly so the tear is fully repaired

steps.whyThisMatters: It draws the line for practice: a person may make these garments wearable again, but the tear itself must stay visible.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
And all of them, one is permitted to tack them together loosely
phrases.notes: 'All of them' means every tear on the ברייתא's list from step 1, the tears that may never be properly mended.

phrases.english: and to hem them and to gather them
and to make them like a kind of ladders,
phrases.notes: He means rough stitches that look like the rungs of a ladder, not a neat seam.

phrases.english: but not to mend them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from how to tear to what may be done with the tear afterward
steps.mimraCoreRuling: These tears may be tacked, hemmed, gathered, or stitched loosely like a ladder, but never mended properly.

steps.title: Introducing a statement of רב חסדא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא introduces רב חסדא, whose statement continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said:
steps.whatsHappening: This line only names the speaker, רב חסדא. The גמרא is setting up his statement, which comes right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No ruling is given yet. The opening words show that a new teaching from רב חסדא is about to be added to this discussion of torn garments.

phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new statement that follows the ברייתא about repairing tears
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ruling itself appears on the next amud.
